headings.title: Introduction and Definition of Coronary Artery Disease
headings.content: Coronary Artery Disease (CAD) is one of the leading causes of morbidity and mortality worldwide and remains a critical focus area for nursing students in Nigeria and globally. CAD is defined as a pathological condition characterized by the narrowing or obstruction of the coronary arteries, which are the vital blood vessels responsible for supplying oxygen-rich blood and essential nutrients to the myocardium. This narrowing typically results from an underlying inflammatory and degenerative process known as atherosclerosis. When the coronary arteries become partially or totally blocked, the heart muscle experiences ischemia, a state of oxygen deprivation. If this oxygen supply-demand imbalance is prolonged, it can lead to myocardial infarction, commonly known as a heart attack, heart failure, or sudden cardiac death. Understanding the definition of CAD lays the fundamental groundwork for clinical assessments, recognizing early warning signs, and delivering effective preventative nursing care to vulnerable patient populations in various healthcare settings.

headings.title: Pathophysiology and Atherosclerosis Development
headings.content: The development of Coronary Artery Disease is deeply rooted in the pathophysiology of atherosclerosis, a complex, progressive inflammatory disease of the arterial walls. The process typically begins in early life with endothelial injury, which can be triggered by factors such as hypertension, smoking, diabetes mellitus, and elevated low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol. Once the endothelial lining is damaged, its permeability increases, allowing circulating LDL particles to penetrate the innermost layer of the arterial wall (the tunica intima) where they become oxidized. This oxidation triggers an immune response, prompting monocytes to migrate into the vessel wall and transform into macrophages. These macrophages engulf the oxidized LDL particles, eventually becoming lipid-laden foam cells. The accumulation of these foam cells creates visible fatty streaks along the arterial walls. Over time, smooth muscle cells migrate from the tunica media to form a fibrous cap over the lipid core, creating an advanced atherosclerotic plaque. As these plaques enlarge, they narrow the arterial lumen and reduce blood flow. Furthermore, plaque rupture or erosion can expose thrombogenic material to the bloodstream, triggering acute platelet aggregation, thrombus formation, and complete occlusion of the coronary vessel.

headings.title: Risk Factors and Etiology
headings.content: A thorough understanding of the risk factors and etiology of Coronary Artery Disease is essential for effective nursing education and disease prevention. Risk factors are broadly classified into non-modifiable and modifiable categories. Non-modifiable risk factors include advanced age, male gender (though the risk for women increases significantly post-menopause), and a positive family history of premature cardiovascular disease, which highlight genetic predispositions. Modifiable risk factors present vital opportunities for nursing interventions and lifestyle modifications; these include cigarette smoking, hypertension, dyslipidemia (high LDL and low HDL cholesterol), diabetes mellitus, obesity, physical inactivity, and chronic psychological stress. Cigarette smoking accelerates atherosclerosis and increases the risk of coronary spasm and thrombosis. Hypertension increases the mechanical workload of the heart and damages the vascular endothelium. Diabetes mellitus promotes accelerated atherogenesis due to metabolic abnormalities and chronic hyperglycemia. By identifying these individual risk factors during patient assessments, nurses can formulate targeted education plans to reduce cardiovascular morbidity and promote healthier lifestyles within communities.

headings.title: Clinical Manifestations: Angina Pectoris and Acute Coronary Syndromes
headings.content: Clinical manifestations of Coronary Artery Disease range from asymptomatic states to severe acute events, primarily categorized as angina pectoris and acute coronary syndromes (ACS). Angina pectoris is chest pain or discomfort resulting from transient myocardial ischemia where oxygen supply is temporarily insufficient to meet myocardial demand. Stable angina is predictable, occurs with physical exertion or emotional stress, and is typically relieved by rest or sublingual nitroglycerin. Conversely, unstable angina is unpredictable, occurs at rest or with minimal exertion, and signifies worsening plaque instability. Acute Coronary Syndromes encompass unstable angina and myocardial infarctions (both NSTEMI and STEMI), which occur when a coronary artery is acutely and severely blocked by a thrombus. Patients experiencing an acute myocardial infarction commonly present with crushing retrosternal chest pain radiating to the left arm, neck, jaw, or back, accompanied by autonomic symptoms such as diaphoresis, nausea, vomiting, shortness of breath, and lightheadedness. Nurses must recognize these symptoms promptly to facilitate rapid triage, diagnostic confirmation, and lifesaving emergency interventions.

headings.title: Diagnostic Evaluation and Investigations
headings.content: Accurate diagnostic evaluation is critical for confirming Coronary Artery Disease, assessing its severity, and guiding appropriate treatment strategies. The 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) is a primary diagnostic tool used to detect ischemic changes, such as ST-segment depression or T-wave inversion in ischemia, and ST-segment elevation in acute myocardial infarction. Cardiac biomarker blood tests, particularly cardiac-specific troponins (Troponin I and T), are essential laboratory investigations because they elevate rapidly when myocardial necrosis occurs. Stress testing, which may involve exercise on a treadmill or pharmacological agents like dobutamine, helps evaluate the heart's response to increased physical demand and unmasks ischemia that may not be apparent at rest. Echocardiography assesses overall cardiac structure, valvular function, and regional wall motion abnormalities indicative of previous or ongoing ischemia. Finally, coronary angiography remains the gold standard diagnostic test for visualizing the exact anatomical location and percentage of stenosis within the coronary arteries using fluoroscopy and radiopaque contrast dye.

headings.title: Medical and Pharmacological Management
headings.content: Medical and pharmacological management of Coronary Artery Disease aims to relieve symptoms, slow disease progression, prevent recurrent cardiac events, and reduce mortality. Antiplatelet medications, such as aspirin and clopidogrel, are foundational in preventing platelet aggregation and subsequent thrombus formation on ruptured plaques. Lipid-lowering agents, particularly statins (e.g., atorvastatin), are prescribed to lower LDL cholesterol, stabilize existing plaques, and exert pleiotropic anti-inflammatory effects on the vascular endothelium. Anti-anginal therapy includes nitrates like sublingual nitroglycerin, which cause systemic vasodilation, reducing preload and myocardial oxygen demand, as well as beta-blockers (e.g., metoprolol) and calcium channel blockers, which decrease heart rate and myocardial contractility. Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) are utilized to manage hypertension, prevent ventricular remodeling, and improve survival, particularly in patients with coexisting heart failure or diabetes. Nurses play a crucial role in educating patients about proper drug administration, monitoring for potential adverse side effects such as hypotension and bleeding, and emphasizing the strict necessity of medication adherence.

headings.title: Surgical Interventions: PCI and CABG
headings.content: When medical management is insufficient to control symptoms or when patients present with high-risk anatomical disease, surgical and interventional procedures are indicated. Percutaneous Coronary Intervention (PCI), which includes balloon angioplasty and stent placement, is a minimally invasive procedure where a catheter is threaded through a peripheral artery (typically femoral or radial) to the site of coronary obstruction. A balloon is inflated to compress the plaque, and a metallic stent is deployed to keep the vessel patent. Conversely, Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting (CABG) is an open-heart surgical procedure where healthy blood vessels—such as the greater saphenous vein from the leg or the internal mammary artery from the chest—are harvested and grafted to bypass blocked coronary arteries, re-establishing adequate blood flow downstream of the occlusion. Nurses must provide meticulous pre-operative preparation, continuous post-procedural monitoring for hemorrhage, dysrhythmias, and graft occlusion, as well as wound care and patient education regarding long-term lifestyle modifications.

headings.title: Nursing Assessment and Patient Care Planning
headings.content: Nursing assessment and comprehensive patient care planning are vital for achieving optimal outcomes in patients diagnosed with Coronary Artery Disease. The nursing assessment begins with a detailed health history focusing on chest pain characteristics (using the OLDCARTS mnemonic), associated symptoms, past medical history, and risk factor identification. Physical assessments involve monitoring vital signs, evaluating heart sounds for murmurs or an S3/S4 gallop, assessing lung fields for crackles indicative of heart failure, and checking peripheral pulses and capillary refill. Nurses prioritize care plans based on immediate physiological needs, formulating diagnoses such as ineffective cardiac tissue perfusion, acute pain, anxiety, and deficient knowledge. Care planning includes administering prescribed medications, managing chest pain protocols promptly, ensuring physical rest during acute phases, and monitoring telemetry for lethal cardiac dysrhythmias. Furthermore, nurses design individualized educational programs that empower patients to adopt heart-healthy diets, engage in safe physical activity, stop smoking, and recognize when to seek emergency medical attention.

headings.title: Complications and Cardiac Rehabilitation
headings.content: Patients with Coronary Artery Disease are at risk for several life-threatening complications, making diligent monitoring and structured cardiac rehabilitation essential components of long-term care. Major complications include acute myocardial infarction, severe heart failure due to impaired pumping ability, cardiogenic shock, and lethal cardiac dysrhythmias such as ventricular fibrillation and ventricular tachycardia. Cardiac rehabilitation is a medically supervised program designed to optimize physical, psychological, and social functioning after a cardiac event or procedure. It consists of three phases: inpatient mobilization, outpatient supervised exercise and monitoring, and long-term independent maintenance. Rehabilitation programs incorporate progressive physical conditioning, nutritional counseling provided by dietitians, stress management techniques, and smoking cessation support. Nurses collaborate closely with multidisciplinary rehabilitation teams to encourage patient compliance, monitor exercise tolerance, reduce psychological depression and anxiety, and ultimately enhance the patient's long-term quality of life and survival rates.
